# Interviewer Guide -- Question 1: Course Number Resolution

**Do not share this file with candidates.**

## Source (internal note)

Drawn from Berkeleytime commit `06dd8d6c8` ("fix: make curated classes
findable by their real course number", #1157), first sub-fix: "fix:
identify curated classes by class subject and number."

Real bug: the admin "curate a class" tool (`CuratedClassEditor`,
`CuratedClasses` list page, `GET_CATALOG` query) read `subject` /
`courseNumber` off the **joined `course` record** instead of the
**`class` record**. Berkeley's SIS renumbers courses (e.g. INTEGBI
32 -> 130), but the stored `course` document keeps the old number until
a separate "FUTURE" version of the course is later promoted over it by
the datapuller. The `class` record, by contrast, already carries the
correct/current `subject`/`courseNumber` at all times. Net effect: a
newly-renumbered course's curated entry displayed and searched under its
stale number and was unfindable by its real one. The stale values were
also what got written into the saved `CuratedClass` document, and the
backend resolves a curated class against `ClassModel` -- so such an entry
would never resolve correctly server-side either.

A second, related bug lived on the curated-classes list page: rows
rendered `{subject} {courseNumber}` but the fuzzy-search index was built
from `{subject} {number}` -- `number` being the **section** number, not
the course number -- so no course number ever matched a search on that
page, independent of the join bug above.

The real fix: select `subject`/`courseNumber` on the `class` in
`GET_CATALOG` (drop the now-redundant `course.subject`/`course.number`
selections), and use the class's fields everywhere identity was
previously read from `course` -- in the search index, the result cards,
and the value saved into the curated class. Two other, unrelated sub-fixes
landed in the same PR (datapuller delete-semantics and partial-fetch
safety) -- out of scope for this question; they're covered by other
questions in this kit.

The starter's fixture data (`crs-integbi-1`/`crs-colwrit-1` lagging,
`crs-math-1` not) is a direct simplification of this real scenario, down
to reusing INTEGBI and COLWRIT as the renumbered examples.

---

## Round 1 discussion guide

Candidates don't need to name all four of these, and may raise a
reasonable variant not listed here -- judge the reasoning, not whether
they hit this exact list.

### Design 1: Read identity off the Listing at query/display time (what BT shipped)

Never join to the Item for subject/number; always read `subject`/
`courseNumber` off the Listing (`class`) record, since it's the one
that's kept current.

- **Pro:** No schema change, no migration, no write-path change. Fixes
  every current and future case as long as the Listing's own fields stay
  current (they're refreshed on every term/offering pull).
  Minimal-diff, matches what was already correct on other parts of the
  system (this is in fact the *cheapest possible* fix, which is exactly
  why BT shipped it).
- **Con:** Doesn't fix anything for entities that have no Listing at
  all, or for a purely catalog-level (no-offering) view that needs a
  correct number and only has the Item to join against. Also doesn't
  help if you need historical/old-number display (see probe below) --
  it discards the old number entirely by not reading it.
- Depends on the *Listing* already being a reliable, current source for
  those fields -- true here because both tables are fed by the same
  upstream pull, but that's an assumption worth surfacing, not a given.

### Design 2: Denormalize category/number onto the Listing at write time

If the Listing doesn't already carry current subject/number, copy them
onto it (or onto a cached identity field) at ingestion time, so no join
is needed at read time.

- **Pro:** Removes a join at read time entirely; read path is trivial.
- **Con:** Write amplification -- every renumbering has to fan out and
  update every dependent Listing row. Consistency window shifts from
  read-time staleness to write-time staleness (the fan-out job itself can
  lag or partially fail). Two copies of the same fact now have to be kept
  in sync forever.
- Good probe: "what enforces that the denormalized copy and the source
  never drift?" A candidate should recognize this needs its own
  idempotent sync job with the same partial-failure hazards discussed in
  the source commit's *other* two sub-fixes (a good candidate may draw
  the parallel unprompted).

### Design 3: Canonical alias/mapping table keyed by a stable internal id

Add a table mapping stable id -> current display number, resolved
through it whenever identity needs to be shown, independent of both Item
and Listing.

- **Pro:** Centralizes "what's the current number for X" as one query,
  reusable by every feature (curation, search, deep links, etc.), and
  naturally supports "formerly known as" by keeping history rows.
- **Con:** Most schema/migration cost of the four. Adds a new table and
  a new source of truth to keep synced with upstream; another place
  identity can drift if the sync job fails silently (exactly the failure
  mode the real PR's second and third sub-fixes were about, for the
  Item table itself).
- Good probe: "who writes to this table, and on what trigger? What
  happens if that writer is behind?" -- this design just relocates the
  staleness problem to a new component unless the candidate specifies its
  own consistency guarantees.

### Design 4: Keep reading from Item, fix propagation to be atomic/immediate

Don't touch the read path; instead make the upstream "future" version
promotion immediate/atomic so Item is never stale.

- **Pro:** Fixes the problem at the actual root cause (the lag), benefits
  every consumer of Item, not just curation.
- **Con:** Usually not fully in your control (upstream system's own
  publish cadence), and "atomic" is doing a lot of work here -- source
  systems like a university SIS batch-publish on their own schedule, and
  "immediate" may not be achievable at all. Even if achievable, doesn't
  eliminate the consistency window, just shrinks it -- there will always
  be *some* moment between a real-world rename and your system reflecting
  it, and something downstream (this curation feature or another) has to
  behave sanely during that moment regardless.
- Good probe if a candidate proposes only this: "the window can't be
  zero. What does curation display during it?" -- forces them back to a
  design in the spirit of 1-3 for the interim, which is a sign they
  understand root-cause vs. defense-in-depth aren't mutually exclusive.

### Follow-up probes for any candidate who lands quickly on one answer

- "What if the source system's renumbering itself has a lag, or fails
  partway (e.g. only some dependent rows get the new number before a
  crash)?" -- tests whether they've thought about partial-write /
  partial-fetch safety, not just the happy path. (The real PR's other two
  sub-fixes are entirely about exactly this: a truncated SIS fetch
  deleting still-valid data.)
- "Does your design need to show the *old* number anywhere (e.g. 'this
  course was formerly numbered X')?" -- Design 1 as stated can't; Designs
  2/3 can if they retain history.
- "What breaks if two Listings for the same Item disagree with each
  other on category/number at the same moment?" (e.g. mid-migration, one
  term's offerings pulled before a renumbering, another after) -- good
  candidates realize this is possible and ask which one "wins" for
  catalog-level (non-offering-specific) display.
- "How would you test this?" -- listen for whether they propose a case
  where Item and Listing *agree* (a control case), not just the
  mismatched case -- a fix that only handles the visibly-broken case can
  still be wrong in a way that happens to look right.

### Red flags

- Never notices that the two entities (Item/course and Listing/class)
  *can* disagree at all -- treats "identity" as a single unambiguous
  fact with one obvious home.
- Proposes a fix with no discussion of tradeoffs -- e.g. "just always
  read from the Listing" with no acknowledgment that this assumes the
  Listing is itself reliably current, or no mention of what happens when
  no Listing exists.
- Doesn't distinguish "fixing the symptom" (read the right field) from
  "fixing the root cause" (why is Item allowed to be stale, and for how
  long) -- fine to prioritize the former for scope reasons, but should be
  named as a choice, not missed entirely.
- Treats this as a one-time data-cleanup task rather than a standing
  invariant that has to hold as new renumberings happen indefinitely.

## Round 2 code review guide

### What the test suite checks

`impl/test/curatedClasses.test.ts`, 8 tests. Both stubbed functions
throw `not implemented`, so all 8 fail until a real implementation is
written. Here's what each verifies about a correct implementation:

1. `buildCatalogOptions` returns the class's real, current
   `subject`/`courseNumber` for two renumbered examples (INTEGBI, COLWRIT)
   -- this requires reading identity off the class (`cls.subject`/
   `cls.courseNumber`), not off the joined course record, since the
   course record can lag after a renumbering.
2. Same function on a *non*-renumbered course (MATH). This is the
   control case: it stops a candidate from special-casing renumbered
   courses, and it's a canary for an implementation that only handles
   the visibly-mismatched examples and happens to look right otherwise.
3. `curateClass` saves the class's real identity, not the course's --
   this follows directly from (1) for any implementation where
   `curateClass` just copies its input, but is worth checking explicitly.
4. `searchCatalog` finds a renumbered class by its current number and
   does *not* still respond to its old number -- exercises the same
   identity-resolution requirement as (1), through the search path.
5. `searchCuratedClasses` (the list page) finds an already-curated entry
   by its course number -- this is a *separate* requirement from (1)-(4):
   it uses fixture data (`curatedClasses` in `data.ts`) that already has
   the correct `courseNumber` saved, so it isolates whether the search
   index is built from `courseNumber` and not `sectionNumber` (a
   different field on the same record), independent of anything about
   `buildCatalogOptions`.

### One correct approach

Design-1-style (matching what Berkeleytime shipped): in
`src/curatedClasses.ts`,

- `buildCatalogOptions` sets `subject: cls.subject` and
  `courseNumber: cls.courseNumber` (not `course.subject`/`course.number`).
- `searchCuratedClasses` builds its searchable name from
  `e.courseNumber` (not `e.sectionNumber`).

That's a small, direct implementation and all 8 tests pass -- verified
locally. It is not the only correct shape: a candidate who instead
pursues Design 2 or 3 from Round 1 will need to touch the fixture shapes
and/or tests themselves (e.g. adding a denormalization step, or an alias
table). A differently-shaped implementation that satisfies the same
underlying properties (renumbered class findable/displayable under its
real, current number; control case still passes; list-page search keyed
on course number) should score the same as the minimal one -- don't
penalize a candidate for not converging on the reference shape. Do check
that they didn't just weaken the tests to make them pass (e.g. deleting
the control-case test, or loosening an assertion) rather than
implementing the underlying behavior. Ask them to walk through *why*
each remaining assertion still holds under their design.

### Questions about AI tool usage

- "What did you ask for first?" -- did they paste the stub and contract
  and ask it to "implement this," or did they first walk it through
  their Round 1 design and ask it to implement *that*? The latter
  suggests they were directing the AI with a plan; the former can still
  produce a correct implementation, worth distinguishing.
- "Did the AI's first draft miss anything?" -- a naive first draft
  commonly gets `buildCatalogOptions` right (it's the more obvious half
  of the contract) but misses that `searchCuratedClasses` needs to key
  off `courseNumber` rather than the more visually-similar
  `sectionNumber` on the same record, since both are plausible "the
  number field" candidates without reading the contract closely. Did the
  candidate catch this themselves, or only because the test suite forced
  it?
- "Did you accept anything you had to later revert or fix?" -- listen for
  self-awareness about a bad suggestion, not just "no, it was perfect."
- "Where did you disagree with a suggestion, and why?" -- a candidate
  with no disagreements across 3-4 hours of AI-assisted work is either
  not reading the output closely or overstating how much they used it.

### Red flags

- Implemented `buildCatalogOptions` correctly but left
  `searchCuratedClasses` reading from the wrong field (or vice versa) --
  i.e., didn't run the full suite, or ran it, saw some green, and stopped
  without checking why others still failed. These are two independent
  requirements on two different functions; an implementation of one says
  nothing about the other, and treating "some tests pass" as "the task is
  done" is the most likely real-world failure mode here.
  - The one thing to be careful reading into this: if the candidate says
    up front "I'm not going to spend time on the list-page path,
    here's why" and explicitly scopes it out, that's a legitimate time
    tradeoff, not the red flag -- the red flag is silently leaving it
    unimplemented while believing the task is done.
- Made the tests pass by editing the test file rather than implementing
  the function, without calling that choice out.
- Can't explain a line of their own implementation when asked -- signals
  copy-pasted AI output with no review.
- No log of AI prompts, or a log that's clearly reconstructed after the
  fact / doesn't match what they describe verbally.

---

## Rubric (1-5 each)

| Dimension | 1 | 3 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|
| System design judgment | Doesn't notice the two entities can disagree; proposes no real design | Proposes one reasonable design, identifies its main tradeoff when prompted | Proposes multiple designs unprompted, reasons about consistency windows and failure modes for each, picks one with a stated justification |
| Code quality/correctness | Fix is wrong, incomplete, or passes tests by weakening them | Fix is correct for the given tests but brittle (e.g. special-cases the broken examples) | Fix is correct, general, and the candidate can articulate why the control-case test still passes |
| Tradeoff articulation | States a design with no tradeoffs, or tradeoffs that don't hold up under a probe | Names at least one real tradeoff (consistency window, write cost, migration cost) per design discussed | Proactively surfaces tradeoffs before being asked, and connects them to concrete failure scenarios (partial upstream fetch, mid-migration disagreement) |
| AI-tool usage judgment | Can't describe what was asked or why; can't explain the resulting diff | Used AI productively but only caught issues when the full test suite forced it | Directed AI with a clear plan, caught a bad/incomplete suggestion independently of the test suite, can articulate specific disagreements |
| Communication | Explanations are hard to follow or contradict the code/design | Clear explanation of what was built and why | Clear, concise, anticipates the interviewer's follow-up questions, distinguishes what they're confident about from what they're guessing at |

## Suggested time budget

- Round 1: 45-60 min (design discussion + probes)
- Round 2: 3-4 hours, done independently/asynchronously before a review
- Round 2 review: 20-30 min (walk the diff, walk the AI prompt log, 2-3
  probes from the red-flag list above)
